Hadamard Gap Theorem

What happens at the boundary when a series has growing gaps?

Exponents doubling like 1, 2, 4, 8 leave bigger and bigger holes. The holes block continuation to every point of the circle. This happens even though the series converges nicely inside. The gap-free comparison series stays calm.

For example, imagine a 🪜 staircase whose steps spread by 1, 2, 4, 8. The first steps are easy. Soon one step is too far, and the wall's end is out of reach.

Unlike the gap series, this sum is continuous on the closed disc, so ∣z∣=1\lvert z \rvert = 1∣z∣=1 is not a natural boundary for the continuous extension (claiming no analytic singularity would go beyond this proof).

Sketch the key idea of the Hadamard gap theorem in 2–3 steps: assuming a holomorphic extension past the boundary, explain the mechanism by which the gaps force a contradiction.

State explicitly in your answer that this is a sketch of the idea, not the complete proof.

Show hint

  1. Start with contradiction: suppose f(z)=∑k≥0z2kf(z) = \sum_{k\ge 0} z^{2^k}f(z)=∑k≥0​z2k extended holomorphically past some boundary point ζ\zetaζ (∣ζ∣=1\lvert \zeta \rvert = 1∣ζ∣=1). Then there is a small disc DDD around ζ\zetaζ on which a holomorphic function agrees with fff inside ∣z∣<1\lvert z \rvert < 1∣z∣<1 — so DDD pokes outside the unit circle.

  2. [IDEA — the step not proved here] Gap-forced overconvergence: the partial sums sk(z)=∑j=0kz2js_k(z) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} z^{2^j}sk​(z)=∑j=0k​z2j converge to fff on ∣z∣<1\lvert z \rvert < 1∣z∣<1, hence to the extension on D∩{∣z∣<1}D \cap \{\lvert z \rvert < 1\}D∩{∣z∣<1}.

    Each new partial sum adds just one term yet leaps twice as far in degree (2k+1=2⋅2k2^{k+1} = 2\cdot 2^k2k+1=2⋅2k) — with no intermediate terms to interfere, a classical overconvergence lemma forces the sequence sks_ksk​ to keep converging uniformly on all of DDD, including points with ∣z∣>1\lvert z \rvert > 1∣z∣>1.

    That lemma is the technical heart; it is stated here, not proved.

But at any point with ∣z0∣>1\lvert z_0 \rvert > 1∣z0​∣>1, sk+1(z0)−sk(z0)=z02k+1s_{k+1}(z_0) - s_k(z_0) = z_0^{2^{k+1}}sk+1​(z0​)−sk​(z0​)=z02k+1​ and ∣z02k+1∣=∣z0∣2k+1→∞\lvert z_0^{2^{k+1}} \rvert = \lvert z_0 \rvert^{2^{k+1}} \to \infty∣z02k+1​∣=∣z0​∣2k+1→∞, so sk(z0)s_k(z_0)sk​(z0​) cannot converge — a contradiction.

    Hence no holomorphic extension past any boundary point exists, and every point of the unit circle is singular.

    To stress again: this is the idea (the skeleton) of the proof, not the complete proof.
